title: Suspend Fundamentals & CPS
scopeHtml: Scope: what suspend means, suspend vs blocking, coroutines vs threads, the CPS transformation, the generated state machine, Continuation/resumeWith, and what "stackless" implies. Interception, suspendCoroutine, ThreadLocals and stack traces are in C1b.

questions.promptHtml: What does the suspend keyword actually do? Does it make a function run in the background?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the most common misconception in Android codebases. Candidates who think suspend means "async" or "background thread" write main-thread jank and ANRs.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: suspend doesn't create a thread and doesn't move work off the main thread. It marks a function that is allowed to pause at suspension points (calls to other suspend functions) without blocking its thread, and resume later, possibly on a different thread. The compiler adds a hidden Continuation parameter so the function can be stopped and restarted. Which thread the code runs on depends on the dispatcher in the coroutine's context, not on the keyword.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A normal function runs from start to finish on the thread that called it. A suspend function can stop in the middle, hand the thread back to its owner, and continue later from the same line with its local variables intact.

Three facts:

  1. It's a capability, not a behaviour. A suspend function that never calls another suspend function never suspends. It runs synchronously on the caller's thread, the same as a normal function. Android Studio flags this as "Redundant 'suspend' modifier".
  2. Suspension happens only at suspension points. These are calls to other suspend functions, ending in a primitive such as delay, withContext, Channel.receive or suspendCancellableCoroutine. Code between two suspension points runs as normal blocking code on whatever thread is current.
  3. The thread comes from the context. A coroutine runs on its CoroutineDispatcher. withContext(Dispatchers.IO) moves work to the IO pool. suspend alone doesn't.
viewModelScope.launch {           // Main thread
    showSpinner()                 // Main
    val user = repo.load()        // suspension point: Main thread is FREE while waiting
    render(user)                  // back on Main (dispatcher re-dispatches)
}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// BROKEN: suspend keyword, but parsing still runs on the caller's thread (Main)
suspend fun parseHugeJson(raw: String): Report = Json.decodeFromString(raw)

// CORRECT: the function itself makes the work main-safe
suspend fun parseHugeJsonSafe(raw: String): Report =
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) { Json.decodeFromString(raw) }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Believing suspend means "runs on IO". It doesn't. The dispatcher decides.
  • Adding suspend to a function "to make it async" when its body has no suspension points. That's a no-op that spreads function colouring.
  • Assuming code after a suspension point runs on the same thread. With multi-threaded dispatchers (Default/IO) it often doesn't.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Can a suspend function run entirely without suspending? → Yes. If no suspension point actually suspends (for example a cache hit), it returns synchronously.
  2. Who decides which thread resumes the coroutine? → The ContinuationInterceptor (the dispatcher) in the context. Details in C1b.
  3. Why can't a normal function call a suspend function? → It has no Continuation to pass. See Q250.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "suspend lets you do async work without blocking". The senior adds that suspend is only a calling convention (hidden continuation param) and does nothing about threads. Main-safety is the job of the function's author, via withContext. A suspend function with no suspension points is synchronous.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams wrap a CPU-heavy suspend fun (JSON parsing, image diffing) and call it from viewModelScope.launch, then wonder why frames drop. The Perfetto trace shows the work sitting on the main thread.

questions.promptHtml: What is the difference between suspending and blocking? Compare delay(1000) with Thread.sleep(1000) inside a coroutine.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It checks whether you understand that coroutines are useful because threads get freed. Without that, everything else (dispatchers, ANRs, starvation) is guesswork.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Blocking holds the thread hostage. Thread.sleep(1000) keeps the OS thread parked for a second, and nothing else can use it. Suspending releases the thread. delay(1000) schedules a resume one second from now and returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, so the thread goes back to the dispatcher and runs other coroutines. On Main, the first freezes the UI. The second doesn't.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Blocking (Thread.sleep, future.get(), sync socket read) Suspending (delay, withContext, await)
Thread during wait Parked, unusable Returned to the dispatcher
Where the "wait state" lives The thread's call stack A heap continuation object
Cost of 10k waiters 10k threads (~1 MB reserved stack each on ART) 10k small objects
Cancellation Only via interrupt, if the code honours it Cooperative: delay throws CancellationException immediately
On Main Frozen frames, ANR after ~5 s of input not handled UI keeps running

How delay works mechanically: it calls suspendCancellableCoroutine, asks the dispatcher's Delay implementation to schedule continuation.resume(Unit) after the timeout (on Android Main that's Handler.postDelayed), and returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. Every frame up the call chain sees that marker and returns too, so the thread unwinds back to its event loop.

Thread.sleep:  [Main thread] ──── blocked 1000 ms ────▶ continue
delay:         [Main thread] return ─ frames, input, other coroutines ─ resume
                       └─ Handler.postDelayed(resume, 1000)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// On Main: freezes UI for 1 s, and cancellation is ignored while sleeping
lifecycleScope.launch { Thread.sleep(1_000); toast() }

// On Main: UI stays responsive; cancelling the scope cancels the wait
lifecycleScope.launch { delay(1_000); toast() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Thinking "it's inside launch, so blocking is fine". launch on Main still runs on Main.
  • Treating Thread.sleep on Dispatchers.IO as harmless. It wastes one of the IO pool's limited threads (64 by default).
  • Assuming suspension is free. It allocates a continuation and re-dispatches. Cheap, but not zero (C1b covers cost).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a Retrofit suspend call blocking? → No. Retrofit enqueues on OkHttp's own threads and resumes the continuation from the callback. The caller's thread is free.
  2. What if a library only offers a blocking API? → Wrap it in withContext(Dispatchers.IO) so a thread built for blocking takes the hit. C1b covers this.
  3. Can a blocking call be cancelled? → Not by coroutine cancellation alone. runInterruptible maps cancellation to Thread.interrupt() (C5).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "suspend doesn't block the thread". The senior explains where the wait state lives (heap continuation vs thread stack), how delay reaches the dispatcher's scheduler and returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, and the knock-on effects on cancellation and pool capacity.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A "retry after 2 s" written with Thread.sleep inside an IO-dispatched coroutine looked harmless. Under a network outage, 64 retries saturated the IO pool and Room queries queued behind them.

questions.promptHtml: Why can a suspend function only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine? Why does it work inside forEach {} but not inside setOnClickListener {}?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It shows whether you know what the compiler does with suspend, beyond "the IDE says no".

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Every suspend function takes a hidden Continuation parameter: the "rest of the computation" to call when it resumes. Only a suspend function or suspend lambda has one to pass. A regular function has no continuation, so the compiler rejects the call. forEach is an inline function, so its lambda body is pasted into the enclosing suspend function and uses that function's continuation. A click listener lambda is a real object invoked later by Android, outside any coroutine, so it can't suspend.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
• The compiler error is "Suspend function 'x' should be called only from a coroutine or another suspend function".
  • Entry points that create a continuation: coroutine builders (launch, async, runBlocking), and the low-level startCoroutine/createCoroutine from kotlin.coroutines.
  • Inline lambdas are allowed because, after inlining, the call sits physically inside the suspend function's body. The rule for regular lambdas matches the rule for non-local return: if a return would be allowed, a suspend call is allowed. noinline and crossinline lambdas may run later, in another frame, so suspension is forbidden there.
  • Non-inline lambdas with a non-suspend function type, such as Sequence.map, Comparator, listeners and Runnable, are all off-limits.
suspend fun sync() {
    items.forEach { api.push(it) }          // OK: forEach is inline → same continuation
    items.asSequence().map { api.get(it) }  // ERROR: Sequence.map lambda is a plain Function1
    button.setOnClickListener { api.x() }   // ERROR: runs later on Main, no continuation
}

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fix for listeners: start a coroutine tied to a lifecycle, don't reach for runBlocking
button.setOnClickListener {
    viewLifecycleOwner.lifecycleScope.launch { viewModel.save() }
}
// Better: send the intent to the ViewModel, which owns the coroutine
button.setOnClickListener { viewModel.onSaveClicked() }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• "Fixing" the error with runBlocking (blocks Main, risks ANR) or GlobalScope.launch (no lifecycle, leaks).
  • Thinking the restriction is a style rule. It's structural: no continuation, nothing to resume.
  • Writing your own higher-order helper without inline and wondering why callers can't suspend inside it. Either make it inline or take a suspend () -> T parameter.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How do I let callers suspend inside my non-inline higher-order function? → Declare the parameter as a suspend function type: fun retry(block: suspend () -> T), and make retry itself suspend.
  2. Can a constructor or property getter be suspend? → No. Constructors, property accessors and some operator conventions can't be suspend. Use a suspend factory function instead.
  3. Why does sequence {} allow yield but not delay? → SequenceScope is @RestrictsSuspension. Inside it, only that scope's own suspend members may be called, so delay is rejected.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "suspend needs a coroutine scope". The senior names the hidden continuation and explains that inlining moves the call into a frame that has one. They also say the fix is to restructure ownership (ViewModel launches), not to bridge with runBlocking.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Code-review classic: someone turns a helper into inline just so callers can suspend inside it, which bloats call sites. A suspend function-type parameter usually does the job more cleanly.

questions.promptHtml: Coroutines are called "lightweight threads". Quantify that. What does a thread cost vs a coroutine, and what happens if you start 100,000 of each on Android?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Senior candidates should back claims with numbers and know where the analogy breaks: coroutines still need threads to run.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: A thread is an OS object with its own native stack. On ART a default java.lang.Thread reserves about 1 MB of virtual stack, plus kernel structures, and creating and context-switching threads costs microseconds of kernel work. A suspended coroutine is just a few heap objects (a Job, its continuation chain and the spilled locals), typically hundreds of bytes. 100k threads on a phone fails with OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create ... failed. 100k coroutines that delay fit in a few tens of MB and run on a handful of threads. But coroutines are multiplexed onto threads, so 100k coroutines doing blocking work are still limited by the thread pool.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
The math (approximate, device-dependent):

Threads:   100,000 × ~1 MB reserved stack     ≈ 100 GB virtual address space
           → 64-bit has the address space, but the kernel/per-process thread limits
             and RSS for touched stack pages kill you long before. Real failure:
             "java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Try again"
             Some OEM ROMs cap threads per process at a few hundred to a few thousand.

Coroutines: 100,000 × (StandaloneCoroutine + continuation + spilled locals)
           assume ~200–500 bytes each      ≈ 20–50 MB heap, all on e.g. 1 Main thread

The per-coroutine size is an estimate. It depends on how many locals are live across suspension and on how deep the suspend call chain is (one continuation object per suspended frame). Measure with a heap dump rather than quoting a constant.

Why coroutines are cheaper:

Aspect Thread Coroutine
Scheduling Preemptive, by the kernel Cooperative, by a user-space dispatcher
Switch cost Kernel context switch A function return plus a queued task
Wait state Whole native stack held Only the live locals, in a heap object
Creation pthread_create syscall Object allocation
Cancellation Interrupt (best effort) Structured, cooperative

Where the analogy breaks:

  • A coroutine is not a thread. It is a resumable computation that borrows a thread between suspension points.
  • CPU-bound coroutines don't gain parallelism beyond Dispatchers.Default's core count.
  • Blocking inside a coroutine pins the borrowed thread, so you're back to thread economics.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Fine: 100k coroutines, each suspended in delay, run on one thread
runBlocking {
    repeat(100_000) { launch { delay(5_000); print(".") } }
}

// Crashes / thrashes: 100k platform threads
repeat(100_000) { thread { Thread.sleep(5_000) } }

(The official kotlinlang "coroutines are light-weight" example uses this pattern. Its count has varied between doc versions, 50k and 100k.)

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Quoting "coroutines are free". 100k concurrent network calls will still overwhelm OkHttp (default maxRequestsPerHost = 5), the server or memory.
  • Comparing launch-and-delay coroutines against threads that block. The fair comparison is with an event loop or callbacks, which coroutines largely are.
  • Forgetting the per-frame continuations: a 10-deep suspend chain means up to 10 continuation objects per suspended coroutine.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. How many threads do coroutines use by default on Android? → Main (1), Default (core count, minimum 2), IO (up to 64 extra, sharing threads with Default). See C3.
  2. Should I launch 10k coroutines to download 10k files? → Launch is cheap, but bound the real work with a Semaphore or limitedParallelism (C8/C3).
  3. Are Kotlin coroutines like Java virtual threads? → Both multiplex many tasks on few carriers, but virtual threads are stackful (whole stack copied out) and transparent to existing blocking APIs. Kotlin coroutines are stackless and compiler-driven. See Q255/Q262.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "coroutines are lighter, you can run thousands". The senior gives the memory math, names the actual ART failure mode, explains why (heap continuation vs native stack, cooperative vs preemptive scheduling) and points out that downstream resources, not coroutine count, are the real limit.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A feed prefetcher that spawned a Thread per image hit pthread_create failed on low-end devices with OEM thread caps. Moving to coroutines removed the crash, but only bounding concurrency fixed the memory spikes. See Q257.

questions.promptHtml: Explain the CPS transformation the Kotlin compiler applies to suspend functions. What does suspend fun getUser(id: String): User look like at the bytecode level?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the classic "do you know how coroutines work under the hood" question, and it separates people who read the docs from people who've read decompiled code.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: CPS means Continuation-Passing Style. The compiler rewrites every suspend function to take an extra last parameter, Continuation<T>, which represents "what to do with the result", and changes its return type to Any?. So getUser(id: String): User becomes getUser(id: String, $completion: Continuation<User>): Any?. The return value is either the real User (it finished without suspending) or the special marker COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, meaning "I've paused, and I'll deliver the result later by calling resumeWith on the continuation you gave me".

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Kotlin source:        suspend fun getUser(id: String): User
JVM signature:        Object getUser(String id, Continuation<? super User> $completion)
                      (Java sees exactly this)

Why Any?: the function has two possible outcomes, and they need one return type.

  1. Completed synchronously. Return the value directly. No resume happens.
  2. Suspended. Return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED (from kotlin.coroutines.intrinsics, an internal enum singleton), and the callee promises to call $completion.resumeWith(...) exactly once later.
  3. Failed synchronously. Throw, as normal.

Call-site protocol: every caller does this check.

val r = getUser(id, myContinuation)
if (r === COROUTINE_SUSPENDED) return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED   // propagate up, freeing the thread
val user = r as User                                         // fast path: keep going

That check cascades: the marker bubbles up every suspend frame to the coroutine's entry point. That entry point is the dispatcher's Runnable, so it returns and the thread is free.

Continuation chain: each suspended function's continuation holds a reference to its caller's continuation (completion). When the innermost one resumes and finishes, it resumes its caller, and so on up the chain. That chain is the heap replacement for a call stack.

Tail-call shortcut: if a suspend call is the last thing a function does (suspend fun a() = b()), the compiler passes its own $completion straight through, with no state machine. Calls in non-tail positions need a state machine (Q253).

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// What you write
suspend fun getUser(id: String): User {
    val token = auth.token()         // suspension point 1
    return api.user(id, token)       // tail-position suspend call
}

// Pseudo-Java of what the compiler emits (simplified)
// Object getUser(String id, Continuation<User> completion) {
//     GetUserSM sm = completion instanceof GetUserSM ? (GetUserSM) completion : new GetUserSM(completion);
//     switch (sm.label) {
//       case 0: sm.id = id; sm.label = 1;
//               Object t = auth.token(sm);
//               if (t == COROUTINE_SUSPENDED) return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED;
//               // fall through with t
//       case 1: String token = (String) (label==1 resumed ? sm.result : t);
//               return api.user(sm.id, token, completion);  // tail: passes completion through
//     }
// }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying CPS "creates callbacks for each line". It creates one continuation object per suspend function invocation (when not tail-only), not per line.
  • Thinking COROUTINE_SUSPENDED is an exception or a thread signal. It's an ordinary return value checked by identity.
  • Assuming Java callers get a nice API. They have to build a Continuation and handle Any? themselves (C1b).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Who allocates the continuation? → The callee allocates its own state-machine object on first entry, wrapping the caller's continuation. On resume it reuses the same object.
  2. Why not just use callbacks? → CPS by the compiler gives sequential code, try/catch/loops across suspension and structured cancellation, without callback hell.
  3. What happens if a function returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED and never calls resume? → The coroutine hangs forever: no thread is held, but the Job never completes. It's a "lost continuation" bug, typical of broken callback wrappers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "the compiler adds a continuation parameter". The senior gives the exact JVM signature, the three-outcome Any? contract, the identity check that cascades the marker up to free the thread, the caller-continuation chain as a heap stack, and the tail-call shortcut.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Teams exposing a Kotlin SDK to Java clients discovered their "nice" suspend API showed up as Object foo(..., Continuation). They had to add CompletableFuture/callback facades.

questions.promptHtml: Walk me through the state machine the compiler generates for a suspend function with two suspension points. What are label, the L$0 fields and invokeSuspend?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: It's the next layer below CPS. Senior candidates can explain how a function "resumes in the middle" and what memory that holds.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: For each suspend function with non-tail suspension points, the compiler generates a continuation class (a subclass of ContinuationImpl). It has an int label saying which suspension point we're at, a result field for the value we resumed with, and fields like L$0, I$0 holding locals that are still needed after the suspension: "spilled" locals. The function body becomes a switch(label). Before each suspension, it saves the live locals into fields, sets the next label and calls the callee. On resume, invokeSuspend(result) calls back into the function, which jumps to the saved label, restores the locals and continues.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
suspend fun loadProfile(id: String): Profile {
    val user = api.user(id)          // suspension point A
    val posts = api.posts(user.id)   // suspension point B
    return Profile(user, posts)
}

Generated (conceptually, the names match real decompiled output):

final class Repo$loadProfile$1 extends ContinuationImpl {
    Object L$0;          // spilled: id or user
    Object result;       // value passed to resumeWith
    int label;           // 0 = start, 1 = after A, 2 = after B
    Object invokeSuspend(Object result) {
        this.result = result;
        this.label |= Integer.MIN_VALUE;     // "I'm a resume, not a fresh call"
        return Repo.this.loadProfile(null, this);
    }
}

loadProfile(id, $completion):
  sm = ($completion is Repo$loadProfile$1 && sign-bit set) ? reuse (clear bit) : new(...)
  switch (sm.label):
    case 0: throwOnFailure(sm.result)
            sm.L$0 = id;  sm.label = 1
            r = api.user(id, sm);  if (r == SUSPENDED) return SUSPENDED
            → goto after_A with r
    case 1: throwOnFailure(sm.result); id = sm.L$0; r = sm.result
    after_A: user = r
            sm.L$0 = user; sm.label = 2
            r = api.posts(user.id, sm); if (r == SUSPENDED) return SUSPENDED
    case 2: throwOnFailure(sm.result); user = sm.L$0; posts = sm.result
            return new Profile(user, posts)

Key mechanics:

  • One object per invocation, reused across resumes. It is allocated on first entry and discarded when the function completes.
  • The sign-bit trick on label distinguishes "re-entering because I'm being resumed" from "a fresh recursive call that happens to receive my continuation type".
  • throwOnFailure(result). If the callee resumed with Result.failure, the exception is rethrown at the suspension point. That's why a normal try/catch around api.user() works.
  • Only live variables are spilled. The compiler does liveness analysis and nulls out dead fields so they don't retain objects (relevant to Q259).
  • Loops. A suspension point inside a loop is still one state. The loop is compiled with jumps back into the switch, so loop counters spill as I$0 etc.
  • BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith runs a loop: when this frame completes, it resumes its completion (the caller's continuation) iteratively rather than recursively, so long chains don't grow the stack on resume.
  • Suspend lambdas compile to a SuspendLambda subclass, where invokeSuspend is the state machine body.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// To see it yourself: Android Studio → Tools → Kotlin → Show Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile
suspend fun two(): Int {
    val a = one()     // label 0 → 1
    val b = one()     // label 1 → 2
    return a + b      // a spilled as I$0 across the second call
}

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "each suspension point allocates a new object". The state machine object is per invocation and reused. Allocation per suspension happens elsewhere (dispatch tasks, CancellableContinuationImpl), covered in C1b.
  • Forgetting that state machine fields keep objects alive while suspended: a big local spilled across a long wait is retained (Q259).
  • Thinking exceptions are delivered "out of band". They're rethrown at the exact suspension point via throwOnFailure.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Why is the label sign bit needed? → Recursion: a suspend function calling itself receives a continuation of its own class. The bit marks a genuine resume vs a new call that must wrap it.
  2. Where are the arguments stored? → Arguments still needed after a suspension spill into L$n fields just like locals.
  3. How does try/finally survive suspension? → Exception table ranges cover the code in every state that lies inside the try. finally code is duplicated on each exit path, so it runs whether the resume carries a value or a failure.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "it becomes a state machine with a label". The senior explains spilling with liveness, object reuse via the sign-bit trick, exception rethrow at the suspension point, loops as a single state, and the iterative resume loop in BaseContinuationImpl. They can also link this to memory retention and debugging.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: Heap dumps of stuck screens often show Foo$bar$1 objects holding L$0 = <Fragment>. Reading those field names tells you exactly which suspension point a leaked coroutine is parked at.

questions.promptHtml: What is the Continuation interface? Explain resumeWith(Result<T>), its context, and the contract a resumer must follow.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Everything else (dispatchers, cancellation, callback bridges) is built on this two-member interface. Seniors should know its contract precisely.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Continuation<in T> has exactly two members: val context: CoroutineContext and fun resumeWith(result: Result<T>). It's the "rest of the program" after a suspension point. You resume it once, with Result.success(value) or Result.failure(exception), and resume/resumeWithException are extension shortcuts for those. The context carries the Job, dispatcher, name and so on. That's how the runtime knows which thread to resume on and whether the coroutine is cancelled. The contract: if a function returned COROUTINE_SUSPENDED, its continuation must be resumed exactly once. Never zero times (hang), never twice (IllegalStateException).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
public interface Continuation<in T> {
    public val context: CoroutineContext
    public fun resumeWith(result: Result<T>)
}
  • in T (contravariant): a Continuation<Any> can accept a String result, so it's safe to use where a Continuation<String> is expected.
  • Why Result<T>: one entry point carries both success and failure. Before Kotlin 1.3's stable coroutines, the experimental API had separate resume/resumeWithException members. 1.3 unified them.
  • context flows down: when a state machine wraps its caller's continuation, it takes context from that completion. So the whole chain shares the coroutine's context. coroutineContext inside a suspend function is an intrinsic that reads exactly this.
  • Who implements it:
    • the compiler-generated state machines (ContinuationImpl, SuspendLambda)
    • AbstractCoroutine (the root launch/async objects, which are both Job and Continuation)
    • CancellableContinuationImpl (what suspendCancellableCoroutine gives you)
    • DispatchedContinuation (wraps resumes so they hop to the dispatcher)

Resume path:

callback thread → cont.resumeWith(Result.success(user))
  → DispatchedContinuation: dispatcher.isDispatchNeeded? → post task to Main
  → [Main] BaseContinuationImpl.resumeWith loop
        invokeSuspend(result) → state machine jumps to saved label
        when the frame completes → resume its completion (caller) … up to the root coroutine
  → root AbstractCoroutine.resumeWith → Job completes → parent notified

Contract rules:

Rule Violation Symptom
Resume exactly once after returning SUSPENDED Never resume Coroutine hangs, Job never completes, screen spinner forever
Resume twice IllegalStateException: Already resumed (on safe wrappers)
Don't resume synchronously from the suspending frame by hand (low-level API) Recursion Stack growth / reentrancy bugs (use suspendCoroutine, C1b)
Respect context Ignore the Job Cancellation doesn't propagate (Q260)

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
import kotlin.coroutines.*

// Create and start a coroutine with a hand-made completion (low-level, stdlib only)
val block: suspend () -> Int = { 40 + 2 }
block.startCoroutine(Continuation(EmptyCoroutineContext) { result: Result<Int> ->
    result.onSuccess { println("done $it") }
          .onFailure { println("failed $it") }   // if you ignore this, failures vanish
})

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Ignoring the failure branch of Result in a hand-written completion. Exceptions disappear silently.
  • Assuming resumeWith runs the rest of the code on the caller's thread. With kotlinx.coroutines it goes through the dispatcher. With raw stdlib APIs and no interceptor, it runs inline on the resuming thread.
  • Calling Result.getOrThrow() on a Result that holds CancellationException and treating it as an error. It's a cancellation signal (C5).

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. What's Continuation(context) { }? → A stdlib factory function that builds a continuation from a lambda. Handy for tests and bridges.
  2. Is Job related to Continuation? → The root coroutine object (StandaloneCoroutine, DeferredCoroutine) implements both. Its resumeWith completing is what completes the Job.
  3. Why must resume-twice be prevented and not just ignored? → The state machine would re-run code from a label with stale spilled state. Later wrappers convert it into a loud IllegalStateException instead of corrupting state (C10 covers callback bridges).

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "continuation is a callback that resumes the coroutine". The senior states the exact two members, why it's Result<T> and in T, how context propagates down the chain, who implements it, and the exactly-once contract with each violation's symptom.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: An analytics SDK bridged a callback API with a raw continuation and resumed on both onSuccess and onComplete. Crashlytics showed Already resumed only on fast networks, where both callbacks fired.

questions.promptHtml: Kotlin coroutines are "stackless". What does that mean, and what are its practical consequences compared to stackful coroutines or virtual threads?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: This is a staff-level design question. It explains why Kotlin has function colouring, inline-only suspension in lambdas, and cheap coroutines, all from one design decision.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Stackless means a suspended coroutine doesn't keep a native call stack. When it suspends, every frame returns (propagating COROUTINE_SUSPENDED), and only the locals each frame needs are saved into heap continuation objects. A stackful design such as Go goroutines or Java virtual threads saves or switches the whole stack, so any function at any depth can suspend. Kotlin's choice has three consequences. It's cheap and needs no runtime/VM support (works on ART, JS, Native). Only functions the compiler transformed, the suspend ones, can suspend: that's function colouring. And a suspend call can't hide inside a non-inline callback or a Java library frame.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Stackful (virtual thread):                 Stackless (Kotlin):
 ┌ frame: libraryCallback()  ┐             frames RETURN on suspend:
 │ frame: blockingRead()     │ ← park:     loadProfile → returns SUSPENDED
 │ frame: yourCode()         │   copy the  api.user    → returns SUSPENDED
 └───────────────────────────┘   stack     heap: [user$SM]→[loadProfile$SM]→[root]
 any frame may park; unmodified            only compiler-transformed frames can be
 Java code just works                      in the chain
Consequence Why it follows from "stackless"
suspend must be declared on every function on the path Each frame must know how to save itself and return the marker
No suspension inside non-inline lambdas / Java callbacks Those frames weren't transformed. They can't return SUSPENDED and be resumed later
Coroutines run anywhere (JVM, ART, JS, Native, Wasm) Pure compiler transformation, no VM stack-switching required
Very cheap suspended state Only live locals are saved, not a 1 MB stack
Calling blocking Java code from a coroutine blocks the thread Unlike virtual threads, the runtime can't intercept Socket.read inside a JDK frame
Resumption rebuilds no stack; frames are re-entered via invokeSuspend The continuation chain is the logical stack. Debug stack traces must be "recovered" (C1b/T2)
Deep non-suspending recursion still uses the native stack Stackless is only about the suspended state. Running frames are normal JVM frames (Q261)

Why Kotlin chose it: coroutines had to ship (Kotlin 1.3, 2018) on existing JVMs and Android with no VM changes, interoperate with Java, and target JS/Native. Stackful coroutines need either VM support (Loom arrived much later, in JDK 21, and isn't in ART) or unsafe stack copying.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Works: inline lambda → same transformed frame
suspend fun a(ids: List<String>) = ids.map { api.get(it) }   // List.map is inline

// Does not compile: Java Executor frame is not transformed
// executor.execute { api.get("1") }   // error: suspend call in non-suspend lambda

// Workaround keeps the boundary explicit
suspend fun b() = withContext(executor.asCoroutineDispatcher()) { api.get("1") }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Saying "stackless means no stack at all". Running coroutine code uses the normal thread stack. Only the parked state is heap-based.
  • Thinking colouring is a language-design accident. It's the price of not needing VM support.
  • Assuming Kotlin coroutines on JDK 21 automatically become virtual threads. They don't. You can use a virtual-thread executor as a dispatcher on server JVMs, but the model stays stackless.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Is a sequence {} builder stackful? → No. It's the same stackless machinery restricted to yield, which is why you can't yield from a nested non-suspend helper.
  2. Why can coroutine stack traces look truncated? → After resume, the thread stack only contains frames from invokeSuspend upward. Callers that are logically "above" exist only as continuation objects. Recovery and debug probes reconstruct them (C1b/T2).
  3. Could Kotlin add stackful coroutines later? → On platforms with VM support (Loom) you can run code on virtual threads alongside coroutines, but changing Kotlin's model would break its multiplatform and interop guarantees. Expect coexistence, not replacement.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "coroutines don't use a thread stack while suspended". The senior derives function colouring, the inline-lambda rule, multiplatform portability, the blocking-Java limitation and stack-trace recovery from the single design choice. They also contrast it precisely with virtual threads.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A team tried to "suspend" inside an OkHttp Interceptor (a Java interface, synchronous by contract). There's no transformed frame there, so they ended up with runBlocking. Knowing why leads to the right design: do the async work before or after the chain, or use OkHttp's own threading.

questions.promptHtml: Does calling a suspend function always suspend? What does a suspend modifier cost if nothing suspends, and when should a function not be suspend?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: API-design judgment. Seniors make functions suspend because of what they do, not by habit, and they know about the synchronous fast path.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: No. A suspend function only suspends if, along its path, some primitive actually returns COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. A cache hit, an already-completed Deferred, withContext to the dispatcher you're already on (it skips the re-dispatch), or a Mutex that's free all return straight away, synchronously. The modifier still has a cost: the hidden parameter, possibly a state-machine allocation per call, and it forces every caller to be suspend. So I make a function suspend only if it actually suspends or will need to (IO, waiting, switching context). Pure computation and getters stay regular functions.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Fast-path examples:

Call Suspends?
deferred.await() on a completed Deferred No: returns the value
withContext(ctx) where ctx has the same dispatcher No dispatch (it runs undispatched), though it's still a cancellation check and scope
mutex.lock() when unlocked No
channel.receive() with an element buffered No
delay(0) No: returns immediately (yield() is the one that always yields)
suspendCancellableCoroutine where the callback fires synchronously before return Resumed before return → no real suspension

Cost of a redundant suspend modifier:

  • Callers: every caller must be suspend or inside a coroutine. Colouring spreads through the codebase and complicates Java/test call sites.
  • Runtime: if the body has non-tail suspend calls, a continuation object is allocated per invocation even when nothing suspends. For a pure function with no suspend calls, the compiler generates no state machine and the overhead is basically the extra parameter. The IDE flags it as a redundant modifier.
  • Semantics: readers assume the function may wait, do IO or switch threads, which misdocuments it.

When to make it suspend:

  • It performs IO, waits for something, or must be main-safe via withContext.
  • It's part of an interface whose implementations will plausibly need to suspend (repository contracts). A suspend interface method is fine even if one fake implementation doesn't suspend.

When not to:

  • Mappers, validators, formatters, UiState reducers: pure and fast.
  • Functions that only start work (fun refresh() in a ViewModel that launches into viewModelScope). Those should be regular functions that return immediately.

sections.label: Code
sections.html:
// Redundant: IDE warning, forces callers to be suspend for nothing
suspend fun formatPrice(cents: Long): String = "%.2f".format(cents / 100.0)

// Right: fast path on cache hit, real suspension on miss
suspend fun user(id: String): User =
    cache[id] ?: withContext(io) { api.user(id) }.also { cache[id] = it }

// ViewModel entry point: NOT suspend; it owns the coroutine
fun onRefresh() { viewModelScope.launch { _state.value = load() } }

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking ViewModel event handlers suspend, which pushes coroutine ownership up to the View.
  • Assuming "it suspended" means a thread hop happened. The fast path keeps you on the same thread in the same call stack.
  • Expecting withContext(sameDispatcher) to yield to other work. It doesn't. Use yield() if you need a cooperative break.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Does a suspend function that doesn't suspend check for cancellation? → Only if it calls something that checks (ensureActive, withContext, yield). The pure fast path doesn't check (C5).
  2. How do you un-colour a suspend API for Java or legacy callers? → Expose a facade: scope.future { } (kotlinx-coroutines-jdk8 / core future), callbacks, or an Rx bridge. Not runBlocking on the main thread.
  3. Is suspend part of the binary API? → Yes. Adding or removing it changes the JVM signature (the extra Continuation param and Object return), so it's a breaking ABI change for library consumers.

sections.label: 3-YOE vs senior answer
sections.html: The average answer is "suspend functions can pause". The senior lists the concrete fast paths, separates the runtime cost (small) from the colouring cost (large), knows suspend is binary-incompatible to add or remove, and has a clear rule: functions that wait are suspend, functions that start work are not.

sections.label: Production connection
sections.html: A library made a Formatter interface method suspend "for future-proofing". Every Compose remember/derivedStateOf call site needed LaunchedEffect plumbing, and removing it later was a breaking ABI change in a major version.

questions.contextHtml:
A social app (4M DAU, 35% of users on devices with 3 GB of RAM or less) has an image prefetcher for its feed. It was written years ago as one Thread per image: thread { download(url); decode(url) }. A new "infinite carousel" feature prefetches up to 300 images per scroll burst. Crash-free users drop from 99.6% to 98.9% within two days of rollout. Top crash:

java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: pthread_create (1040KB stack) failed: Try again
    at java.lang.Thread.nativeCreate(Native Method)
    at java.lang.Thread.start(Thread.java:...)
    at com.app.feed.Prefetcher.prefetch(Prefetcher.kt:41)

It's concentrated on two OEM brands. A teammate notes Java heap usage at crash time is only 120 MB of a 512 MB largeHeap. Another teammate proposes "just switch to GlobalScope.launch, coroutines are lightweight".
questions.promptHtml: Diagnose this, evaluate the proposal, and give the fix.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "It's an OOM, so there's a bitmap leak. Run LeakCanary and add largeHeap." Or: "Coroutines are lightweight, so replace thread {} with GlobalScope.launch {}." The first misreads the error: Java heap is fine, and it's thread creation that failed. The second removes the thread explosion but keeps unbounded concurrency, adds lifecycle leaks, and moves the pressure onto memory and the network.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Thread count at crash time? (Crashlytics custom key, or /proc/self/status Threads:). This confirms thread exhaustion vs heap.
    • Which OEM ROMs and OS versions? Some vendors impose low per-process thread limits.
    • Does the prefetcher run on Main-triggered scroll callbacks? It affects the dispatcher choice.
    • What's OkHttp's dispatcher configuration? (Default is 64 max requests, 5 per host.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Remote-config kill switch to cap carousel prefetch at 10, or disable it on the affected OEMs. Ship a hotfix that routes prefetch through a fixed Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4) if a coroutine refactor can't be reviewed safely in a day.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Thread exhaustion. 300 images × 1 thread each, plus the app's ~150 baseline threads, exceeds the vendor cap. Each thread reserves ~1 MB of stack (the message even says 1040 KB). The error text says pthread_create, not "Failed to allocate".
    2. Virtual address or native memory pressure: 300 × 1 MB = ~300 MB of reserved stack on 32-bit-process devices (if any armeabi-v7a users remain) can exhaust address space.
    3. A bitmap leak (red herring: Java heap is at 120/512 MB, and bitmap pixels live in native memory on API 26+, but the failing call is thread creation).
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • Reproduce on an affected device: scroll the carousel, and watch adb shell ps -T -p <pid> | wc -l and the Android Studio Profiler's thread view.
    • A Perfetto trace shows hundreds of short-lived Thread-NNN.
    • The Memory profiler's native track checks hypothesis 2. LeakCanary checks 3.
  5. Root cause: One OS thread per task. Threads are expensive kernel objects with a reserved native stack, and the per-process limit is hit before the heap is.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: a bounded executor.
    • Long-term: coroutines, owned by a real scope, with bounded concurrency. Coroutines make waiting cheap. They don't make the work free.
    class Prefetcher(
    private val scope: CoroutineScope,          // injected app/feature scope, not GlobalScope
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher,
) {
    private val permits = Semaphore(6)            // bound real concurrency (C8)
    fun prefetch(urls: List<String>) = urls.forEach { url ->
        scope.launch(io) { permits.withPermit { download(url); decode(url) } }
    }
}
    300 launched coroutines cost a few hundred bytes each (~300 × ~0.5 KB ≈ 150 KB) and run on IO pool threads, of which at most 6 are busy. Better still, delegate to the image library (Coil/Glide), which already pools and dedups, and cancel prefetch when the carousel leaves the screen.
  7. Prevention: A lint/detekt rule banning thread {} and Thread(...).start() outside an allow-list. A thread-count gauge in performance monitoring. Low-RAM devices from the affected OEMs added to the device lab.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not GlobalScope (no cancellation when the user leaves, so prefetches keep downloading). Not unbounded launch (300 parallel decodes = native memory spike and 5-per-host queueing anyway). Not largeHeap (it doesn't touch thread limits).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why not just limitedParallelism(6) instead of a Semaphore?" → Also valid. It bounds threads used for the work. Semaphore bounds the critical section regardless of dispatcher. Either works here (C3/C8 cover the nuances).
  • "Would the 300 coroutines all run in parallel on IO?" → Up to the IO pool limit (64 by default). Without a bound you'd still get 64 concurrent decodes.
  • "Why did only two OEMs crash?" → Vendor thread caps and kernel limits vary. Stock Android allows far more threads per process.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: On a past team, a "fire a thread per upload" helper crashed only on one vendor's budget line. The fix that stuck wasn't the coroutine rewrite. It was the 4-permit bound, which also cut upload p95 because uploads stopped competing for bandwidth.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: blames heap or bitmaps, proposes largeHeap or GlobalScope.
  • Hire: identifies thread exhaustion from pthread_create, moves to coroutines with a proper scope.
  • Strong hire: quantifies thread vs coroutine cost, bounds concurrency explicitly, explains that coroutines fix the waiting cost but not the work cost, and adds lint plus monitoring.

questions.contextHtml:
A PR migrating a sync engine from callbacks to coroutines fails to compile. The author "fixed" it and requests review. The original attempt:

suspend fun syncAll(ids: List<String>): List<Item> =
    ids.asSequence()
        .filter { it.isNotBlank() }
        .map { api.fetch(it) }                  // error: suspension functions can be called
        .toList()                               // only within coroutine body

class ItemComparator : Comparator<Item> {
    override fun compare(a: Item, b: Item): Int =
        priorityOf(a) - priorityOf(b)           // priorityOf is `suspend` (reads DataStore)
}

The "fixed" version in the PR:

suspend fun syncAll(ids: List<String>): List<Item> =
    ids.asSequence().filter { it.isNotBlank() }
        .map { runBlocking { api.fetch(it) } }.toList()

class ItemComparator : Comparator<Item> {
    override fun compare(a: Item, b: Item): Int =
        runBlocking { priorityOf(a) - priorityOf(b) }
}

syncAll is called from viewModelScope.launch {} (Main.immediate). The sync list is ~400 items. Sorting 400 items does ~3,500 comparisons.
questions.promptHtml: What's wrong with the fix, why did the original fail to compile, and how would you rewrite it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Compiles now, and runBlocking is inside a suspend function, so it's fine." Or: "Use GlobalScope.launch inside map." Both miss that runBlocking blocks the calling thread (here Main), and that the problem is structural: these lambdas aren't transformed frames.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Should fetches be sequential or parallel? (Server rate limits?)
    • Is priority stable during a sort, or can it change mid-sort?
    • Which dispatcher do api.fetch and priorityOf use internally?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Block the merge. This would freeze Main for the duration of 400 sequential network calls (at 150 ms each, that's 400 × 0.15 = 60 s), a certain ANR. The comparator does ~3,500 DataStore reads, each under runBlocking.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (why the original fails):
    1. Sequence.map is not inline. Its lambda compiles to a plain (T) -> R function object, invoked later by the sequence iterator, so there's no continuation to suspend with. (List.map is inline and would compile.)
    2. Comparator.compare is a Java interface method. It's not a suspend function, and sortedWith calls it from non-transformed stdlib frames.
    3. Red herring: "a missing import or wrong scope". It's not scoping. It's that stackless coroutines can only suspend in compiler-transformed frames.
  4. How I'd verify each: Check the declarations of Sequence.map and List.map (no inline vs inline). Run on a device with StrictMode and the Profiler: the main thread is blocked inside BlockingEventLoop under runBlocking. The ANR trace shows kotlinx.coroutines.BlockingCoroutine.joinBlocking on main.
  5. Root cause: The suspend calls sit in non-inline, non-suspend lambdas. The "fix" bridges by blocking the current thread, which is Main here, and nests event loops, defeating the point of coroutines.
  6. Fix: 
    // 1) Use inline collection ops (or a Flow) so the call stays in the suspend frame
suspend fun syncAll(ids: List<String>): List<Item> =
    ids.filter { it.isNotBlank() }.map { api.fetch(it) }      // sequential, compiles

// 1b) Parallel with a bound if the server allows (C2/C8 cover details)
suspend fun syncAllParallel(ids: List<String>): List<Item> = coroutineScope {
    val gate = Semaphore(8)
    ids.filter { it.isNotBlank() }
       .map { id -> async { gate.withPermit { api.fetch(id) } } }
       .awaitAll()
}

// 2) Never suspend inside a comparator: resolve the keys first, then sort purely
suspend fun sortByPriority(items: List<Item>): List<Item> {
    val prio = items.associateWith { priorityOf(it) }        // 400 reads, not ~3,500
    return items.sortedBy { prio.getValue(it) }
}
    Comparing via prio[a] - prio[b] subtraction would also risk Int overflow, so I'd use sortedBy/compareBy.
  7. Prevention: Detekt or a custom lint rule flagging runBlocking outside main()/tests. A review checklist item: "suspend calls inside non-inline lambdas → restructure, never bridge". A StrictMode detectAll() thread policy in debug builds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not GlobalScope.launch inside map (fire-and-forget, results lost, no cancellation). Not asFlow().map {} just to keep the sequence shape. It works (Flow's map takes a suspend lambda), but a plain list is simpler for a finite batch.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why does List.map { api.fetch(it) } compile but Sequence.map doesn't?" → List.map is inline, so the lambda body is pasted into syncAll's state machine. Sequence.map stores the lambda for lazy evaluation.
  • "What if a third-party library only gives you a non-inline callback API?" → Wrap it at the boundary with suspendCancellableCoroutine/callbackFlow (C10). Don't block.
  • "Is runBlocking inside a suspend function ever OK?" → Practically never. It blocks the current thread and ignores the outer coroutine's dispatcher. On a single-threaded dispatcher it can deadlock.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: I've seen a runBlocking comparator survive review because tests ran on JVM threads. On a device, a 2,000-item sort took 9 s on Main and produced an ANR cluster the week it shipped. The fix was one associateWith line.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: accepts runBlocking or suggests GlobalScope.
  • Hire: explains inline vs non-inline lambdas and rewrites with List.map, noting the Main-thread blocking.
  • Strong hire: explains it via stackless/transformed frames, precomputes comparator keys (cutting ~3,500 reads to 400), offers bounded parallelism, and adds lint/StrictMode prevention.

questions.contextHtml:
A document-scanning app uploads multi-page scans. On 2 GB RAM devices (22% of 1.1M MAU), the OS kills the process in the background during uploads: low-memory kills rise 3x after a release. The upload code:

suspend fun uploadScan(scanId: String) {
    val pages: List<ByteArray> = store.loadPages(scanId)     // ~12 pages × 3 MB = ~36 MB
    val pdf: ByteArray = pdfEncoder.encode(pages)            // ~25 MB
    val receipt = api.upload(scanId, pdf)                    // p95 = 40 s on 3G
    analytics.track("uploaded", pages.size, receipt.id)      // uses pages after the wait
    notifyUser(receipt)
}

A heap dump taken during api.upload shows ScanRepo$uploadScan$1 retaining 61 MB through fields L$0, L$1, L$2. A teammate says "the GC will collect pages once encoding is done, so the dump must be from a debug build". Another suggests adding System.gc() after encoding. The build that produced the dump is a release build (R8 on).
questions.promptHtml: Explain what the heap dump is telling you, and fix the memory profile.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Add System.gc(), or call pages = emptyList()." Or "use largeHeap". These treat it as a GC problem. In reality the code keeps live references in the continuation object for the full 40 s upload, and vals can't be reassigned anyway.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • What exactly are L$0..L$2 in the dump? (Inspect their types: String, ArrayList<byte[]>, byte[].)
    • Does api.upload need the whole ByteArray, or can it stream from a file?
    • Was the dump from a build compiled with -Xdebug? That flag (Kotlin 1.8+) disables the compiler's liveness optimization of spilled variables so the debugger can show them. I'd confirm the release build doesn't set it.
  2. Immediate mitigation: Gate multi-page upload behind a size threshold on low-RAM devices (ActivityManager.isLowRamDevice / memoryClass). Move uploads into WorkManager so a killed process retries instead of losing the work.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Spilled locals are genuinely live. pages is used after the api.upload suspension point (pages.size in analytics), so the compiler must spill it into the state machine. pdf is passed into upload, and OkHttp's RequestBody holds it for the duration anyway. Plus scanId. Total ≈ 36 + 25 = 61 MB, which matches the dump.
    2. A debug-flagged build kept dead variables alive. That's plausible in general, but here hypothesis 1 already explains every byte, and the build is release.
    3. A leak in pdfEncoder (red herring: the retaining path goes through the continuation's fields, not the encoder).
  4. How I'd verify each: In the Android Studio Memory Profiler (heap dump), select the byte[] instances and look at "References" → ScanRepo$uploadScan$1.L$1. Decompile the function (Show Kotlin Bytecode → Decompile) to see which variables are stored before the upload call. Then a test build with the fix, comparing the Java heap graph during upload.
  5. Root cause: In a stackless coroutine, every local that's live across a suspension point is a field of the heap continuation object. While suspended for 40 s, that object (reachable from OkHttp's callback → CancellableContinuation → state machine) pins those values. The GC is doing its job. The program still references them.
  6. Fix: Shrink what's live across the long suspension, then stream instead of buffering. 
    suspend fun uploadScan(scanId: String) {
    val pdfFile: File = encodeToFile(scanId)          // pages loaded & released inside
    val pageCount = pdfFile.pageCountMeta              // capture a primitive, not the list
    val receipt = api.upload(scanId, pdfFile.asRequestBody("application/pdf".toMediaType()))
    analytics.track("uploaded", pageCount, receipt.id) // only an Int spilled (I$0)
    notifyUser(receipt)
}

private suspend fun encodeToFile(scanId: String): File = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
    val pages = store.loadPages(scanId)       // live only within this frame; no suspension
    pdfEncoder.encodeTo(pages, tempFile(scanId)) // after it, so nothing spilled
}
    Peak during upload: from ~61 MB down to an OkHttp streaming buffer (a few KB to tens of KB). Encoding still peaks at ~36 MB briefly, but not for 40 s.
  7. Prevention:
    • A review checklist item: "large objects must not be live across long suspension points (network, user input, delays)".
    • A macrobenchmark/memory test with a fake 40 s upload asserting a Java-heap ceiling.
    • Production memory telemetry (Debug.getPss/ApplicationExitInfo with REASON_LOW_MEMORY, API 30+).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not System.gc() (it can't collect reachable objects). Not making pages a nullable var and setting it to null (it works, but it's fragile and hides intent; scoping is cleaner). Not largeHeap (it doesn't help background LMK priority). Writing to a temp file costs IO and needs cleanup on cancellation (C5 covers finally handling).

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "If pages weren't used after upload, would it still be retained?" → In a normal build, no. Liveness analysis wouldn't spill it, or the field would be cleared. With -Xdebug it may be kept alive, which is why you shouldn't take memory measurements from such builds.
  • "Does R8 change any of this?" → R8 optimises bytecode but doesn't restructure the coroutine state machine's spilling semantics. Don't rely on it to drop live fields.
  • "How does this differ for threads?" → With a blocking thread, the same locals would sit on that thread's stack frame, with the same retention. Coroutines just make it visible as named heap fields.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A "retry upload after 30 s delay" loop kept a decoded 20 MB bitmap spilled across delay(30_000). Moving the decode inside the retry attempt cut background LMK kills on low-end devices by more than half.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests System.gc()/largeHeap, can't explain L$0.
  • Hire: recognises spilled locals across the suspension point and narrows scope.
  • Strong hire: maps fields to variables via decompile and heap-dump references, does the math, mentions liveness and -Xdebug, and streams the upload so nothing large spans the wait.

questions.contextHtml:
A game-engine SDK team (embedded in 30+ partner apps) exposes a Kotlin scripting hook. Partners write suspend scripts, and the SDK runs them from its frame loop using only stdlib APIs, to avoid a kotlinx.coroutines dependency:

fun runScript(script: suspend () -> Unit) {
    script.startCoroutine(Continuation(EmptyCoroutineContext) { result ->
        if (result.isSuccess) log("script ok")
    })
}

Partner scripts use kotlinx.coroutines internally (delay, withContext(Dispatchers.IO), ensureActive()). Post-incident findings after a partner escalation:

  • Scripts kept running after the user left the level. CPU and battery use stayed up for minutes (one partner reported 9% extra battery per hour).
  • ensureActive() calls in scripts "never fire".
  • A crash in a script (IOException) never appeared in Crashlytics. The level just silently didn't load.
  • Code after delay() ran on a kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor thread and touched engine state that isn't thread-safe. A rare native crash appeared (SIGSEGV in engine::Scene::update).
questions.promptHtml: Lead the post-incident review. Explain each finding mechanically and propose the design.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Use GlobalScope.launch instead" or "add try/catch in scripts". That doesn't explain why the context matters and treats symptoms partner by partner.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Must the SDK stay free of a kotlinx.coroutines dependency? (Partners already pull it in.)
    • Is the engine single-threaded? Which thread owns the Scene?
    • What lifetime should a script have: per level, per session?
    • Do partners need results or errors surfaced to them?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Ship an SDK patch that wraps the script in try/catch(Throwable) and reports via the partner error callback. Add a kill flag the frame loop checks. Publish guidance: "touch Scene only via engine.post {}".
  3. Hypotheses, ranked (each finding mapped to the Continuation contract):
    1. No Job in context. EmptyCoroutineContext has no Job, so nothing can cancel the coroutine. coroutineContext.ensureActive() is defined as get(Job)?.ensureActive(), which is a no-op without a Job, and isActive returns true. That explains finding 1 and finding 2.
    2. The completion ignores Result.failure. resumeWith is the only place a terminal exception is delivered. The lambda only logs success, so failures vanish. That's finding 3. There's also no CoroutineExceptionHandler or parent to propagate to, since this isn't a kotlinx coroutine.
    3. No ContinuationInterceptor. With no dispatcher in the context, delay uses kotlinx.coroutines' default delay implementation and resumes the continuation on its internal DefaultExecutor thread. Without an interceptor, resumption runs inline on whatever thread calls resumeWith. That's finding 4.
    4. Red herring: "the engine's native code is buggy". The SIGSEGV is a symptom of off-thread access.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A unit test with a fake script: println(coroutineContext[Job]) prints null. Thread.currentThread().name after delay shows kotlinx.coroutines.DefaultExecutor.
    • The coroutine debug agent (DebugProbes.dumpCoroutines()) shows the scripts still alive after the level exits.
    • A Perfetto trace shows the CPU work after the level exits.
  5. Root cause: A Continuation's context is the coroutine's identity: lifetime (Job), threading (interceptor), naming and error handling. The completion's resumeWith is its only exit. The SDK supplied an empty context and a completion that drops failures, so it opted out of cancellation, thread confinement and error reporting.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term (stdlib-only), if the dependency rule really holds: supply a real context. Build a minimal ContinuationInterceptor that posts resumes to the engine thread, and a cancellation flag the frame loop and scripts check. Make the completion report result.exceptionOrNull(). This re-implements kotlinx poorly, so I'd time-box it.
    • Long-term: depend on kotlinx.coroutines (partners already ship it) and give each level a proper scope.
    class LevelScripts(engineDispatcher: CoroutineDispatcher, private val onError: (Throwable) -> Unit) {
    private val scope = CoroutineScope(
        SupervisorJob() + engineDispatcher + CoroutineName("level-scripts") +
        CoroutineExceptionHandler { _, e -> onError(e) }
    )
    fun run(script: suspend CoroutineScope.() -> Unit) = scope.launch(block = script)
    fun onLevelExit() = scope.cancel()   // cancels every script; ensureActive now works
}
// engineDispatcher: e.g. a Handler(engineLooper).asCoroutineDispatcher(),
// so code after delay() resumes on the engine thread
  7. Prevention:
    • An API-review rule: no startCoroutine/createCoroutine with EmptyCoroutineContext in production code.
    • A contract test suite for the hook: cancellation on exit, error surfacing, resume-thread assertion.
    • Thread assertions in Scene (check(Looper.myLooper() == engineLooper)) in debug builds.
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not GlobalScope (it adds a dispatcher but still has no lifetime). Not catching exceptions inside every partner script (it pushes the SDK's responsibility onto 30 teams). Adding the kotlinx dependency costs some APK size, but partners already pay it, so the marginal cost is about zero.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Why did withContext(Dispatchers.IO) work at all with no Job?" → withContext creates its own scoped coroutine. The missing parent Job only means there's nothing upstream to cancel it.
  • "Could you make ensureActive work without kotlinx?" → Only by putting your own Job-like element in the context, and kotlinx's ensureActive only understands kotlinx Job. That's another argument for the dependency.
  • "What if the completion threw?" → It would propagate on whatever thread called resumeWith, here the DefaultExecutor, probably crashing the app with a confusing trace.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A plugin host I reviewed started coroutines with startCoroutine and an empty context "for minimalism". Three teams independently reinvented cancellation flags before someone traced every bug back to the one missing Job in the context.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: suggests GlobalScope or partner-side try/catch, without explaining context.
  • Hire: identifies the missing Job and dropped failure, and proposes a scoped launch.
  • Strong hire: maps all four findings to Continuation's context and resumeWith contract (Job, interceptor, completion), explains why ensureActive is a no-op, designs a per-level scope with an engine dispatcher, and adds contract tests.

questions.contextHtml:
A notes app renders nested comment threads. A recursive suspend loader worked fine for 2 years with threads at most ~200 replies deep:

suspend fun loadThread(id: String): Node {
    val c = dao.comment(id)                       // Room suspend; usually a cache hit
    val kids = c.childIds.map { loadThread(it) }  // recursion
    return Node(c, kids)
}

A B2B customer imports a ticket-system export with one reply chain 12,000 deep (a 10x+ jump in depth). Crashlytics:

java.lang.StackOverflowError: stack size 1039KB
    at com.app.ThreadRepo.loadThread(ThreadRepo.kt:12)
    at com.app.ThreadRepo.loadThread(ThreadRepo.kt:13)
    ... (repeats)

It only occurs on Dispatchers.Default worker threads, never on Main. A teammate argues: "Coroutines are stackless. They can't stack-overflow. This must be a Room bug." Another proposes running the loader on a custom Thread with a 64 MB stack.
questions.promptHtml: Explain why a "stackless" coroutine overflowed, and fix it for arbitrary depth.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Increase the stack size" or "add yield() somewhere". Both lack the mechanism. A bigger stack just moves the cliff, and an ad-hoc yield happens to work by accident without the candidate knowing why.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Max realistic depth and total node count?
    • Do we need the whole tree in memory, or is it rendered lazily?
    • Is dao.comment a cache hit (no real suspension) most of the time?
    • Why only on Default? (Hint: Main has a bigger stack, about 8 MB on Android.)
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cap the render depth at, say, 500 with "continue thread" pagination for that customer. Catch StackOverflowError at the loader boundary to show an error state instead of crashing. (This is a temporary guard. Catching Errors isn't a design.)
  3. Hypotheses, ranked:
    1. Non-suspending recursion uses the native stack. "Stackless" describes the suspended state only. When dao.comment returns synchronously (an in-memory/Room fast path, or no actual suspension), loadThread calls itself as an ordinary JVM call. Each level pushes a JVM frame plus allocates a state machine. Math: 12,000 levels × roughly 80–100 bytes of frame (loadThread, map inlined, locals) ≈ 1 MB, right at the ~1 MB worker-thread limit. The 8 MB Main stack hides it, which explains "never on Main".
    2. Even when it does suspend, resume doesn't rebuild the stack, but the next descent starts fresh from invokeSuspend and recurses down again until the next real suspension.
    3. Red herring: a "Room bug". The trace is entirely loadThread frames.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A JVM unit test with a fake DAO that returns immediately (no suspension) and depth 12,000. It reproduces deterministically.
    • Make the fake DAO yield() each call: the overflow disappears, confirming that the crash depends on depth without suspension.
    • The frame count in the trace confirms it.
  5. Root cause: Stackless coroutines save heap state only when frames return COROUTINE_SUSPENDED. Deep recursion that completes synchronously at each level is plain recursion on the thread stack, and the stack overflows like any recursive function.
  6. Fix:
    • Short-term: an iterative traversal with an explicit heap-allocated work stack, which removes recursion entirely.
    suspend fun loadThread(rootId: String): Node {
    val comments = HashMap<String, Comment>()
    val stack = ArrayDeque<String>().apply { add(rootId) }
    while (stack.isNotEmpty()) {
        val c = dao.comment(stack.removeLast())        // suspend calls are fine in loops
        comments[c.id] = c
        c.childIds.forEach(stack::addLast)
    }
    return buildTree(rootId, comments)                 // build bottom-up, iteratively too
}

// Bottom-up assembly without recursion: post-order via two stacks
private fun buildTree(rootId: String, byId: Map<String, Comment>): Node {
    val order = ArrayList<String>(byId.size)
    val st = ArrayDeque<String>().apply { add(rootId) }
    while (st.isNotEmpty()) { val id = st.removeLast(); order += id; byId.getValue(id).childIds.forEach(st::addLast) }
    val built = HashMap<String, Node>(byId.size)
    for (id in order.asReversed()) { val c = byId.getValue(id); built[id] = Node(c, c.childIds.map { built.getValue(it) }) }
    return built.getValue(rootId)
}
    • Alternative: keep the recursive shape but move frames to the heap with stdlib DeepRecursiveFunction (experimental in Kotlin 1.4, stable since 1.7). It's built on the same stackless machinery: callRecursive "suspends" each level into heap continuations. It isn't a coroutine you can call dao from, though, because its scope is @RestrictsSuspension. So I'd load the data first, then use it for pure tree building.
    • Long-term: batch the query. One Room query with a recursive CTE (WITH RECURSIVE) returns all descendants, which replaces 12,000 DAO calls with one. Then render lazily (a flattened LazyColumn with an indent level) so a 12k-deep tree never needs a 12k-deep composable hierarchy either.
  7. Prevention:
    • Property-based tests with deep and degenerate trees (a linked list, 50k deep).
    • A max-depth assertion in import pipelines.
    • Code review: "recursion depth driven by user data → iterative or DeepRecursiveFunction".
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not a 64 MB custom thread stack (it moves the cliff, wastes memory, and is a dedicated thread outside the dispatcher). Not sprinkling yield() to "force" heap frames (it does avoid the overflow, since each level returns SUSPENDED, but it adds 12,000 dispatches and documents nothing). Iterative code is less elegant but has predictable memory: O(nodes) on the heap.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "So why does yield() fix it?" → Each level actually suspends, so every frame returns and the depth lives in heap continuations. Resume goes through BaseContinuationImpl's iterative loop, not recursion. It's correct mechanically, but slow and obscure.
  • "Does tailrec help?" → No. tailrec doesn't apply here: the recursive call isn't in tail position (results feed map), and the tree has multiple children per node.
  • "Would the same crash happen with real IO suspension every level?" → Mostly not, but you'd allocate 12k continuation objects held in one chain: heap, not stack, and still a sign the algorithm needs batching.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A folder-sync feature crashed only for one enterprise customer with auto-generated 20k-deep directory nests. Everyone assumed coroutines made recursion "safe". The iterative rewrite plus a single recursive SQL query fixed the crash and cut load time from 14 s to under 1 s.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: "coroutines can't overflow", or a bigger stack.
  • Hire: explains that synchronous completion means native recursion, and rewrites iteratively.
  • Strong hire: does the depth × frame-size math, explains the Main vs worker stack difference, knows DeepRecursiveFunction and its restricted scope, and fixes the data access (recursive CTE) and rendering too.

questions.contextHtml: Your company is building a Kotlin Multiplatform "core" module shared by the Android app (minSdk 26, 6M MAU), the iOS app, and a JVM backend service on JDK 21. The backend lead proposes: "Let's drop coroutines from the shared module. JDK 21 virtual threads let us write plain blocking code that scales to millions of tasks, with no suspend colouring, and stack traces are normal. Android can just use a thread pool." The shared module has about 140 repository/use-case functions. 90 are currently suspend, and 40 expose Flow.
questions.promptHtml: Evaluate the proposal and give a recommendation for each platform.

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: "Coroutines are better because they're lightweight" or "virtual threads are newer, so use them". Neither engages with stackful vs stackless, platform support, or the cost of migrating 90 suspend APIs.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask:
    • Does the shared module run on all three platforms, or only on JVM + Android?
    • What does the backend actually block on? (JDBC, which benefits from virtual threads, vs already-async HTTP.)
    • How many concurrent tasks does Android actually need? (Typically tens, not millions.)
    • Are there Flow consumers in Compose/SwiftUI that can't simply become blocking calls?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Not an incident. I'd freeze the API surface while we decide, and prototype one backend endpoint each way to get real latency numbers.
  3. Hypotheses (options), ranked:
    1. Keep stackless coroutines in shared code, and use virtual threads as a dispatcher on the backend. Shared code stays suspend/Flow. On JDK 21 the backend can run blocking JDBC on Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher(). Each platform gets its best mechanism. This is my pick.
    2. Blocking API plus virtual threads everywhere. This fails on two of three targets. To my knowledge ART doesn't implement Loom virtual threads (verify against the current Android release before relying on that), and Kotlin/Native on iOS has no JVM at all. Android would fall back to platform threads, at about 1 MB of stack each, with no structured cancellation and Main-thread blocking risk.
    3. Dual APIs (blocking for the backend, suspend for mobile). This doubles 140 functions and their tests, and the two copies drift.
  4. How I'd verify each:
    • A prototype benchmark: the backend endpoint with (a) coroutines + Dispatchers.IO + JDBC, (b) coroutines + a virtual-thread dispatcher, (c) plain virtual threads. Measure p95 latency and memory at the target concurrency.
    • On Android: Macrobenchmark and Perfetto for a screen load using the current suspend APIs vs a thread-pool version (cancellation behaviour on back-press is the key difference).
    • Check virtual-thread pinning issues (synchronized blocks and native frames pin the carrier on JDK 21) in the backend's JDBC driver.
  5. Root cause of the disagreement (mechanism):
    Stackful: virtual threads Stackless: Kotlin coroutines
    Can suspend in any frame (incl. JDK blocking IO) Yes: the runtime parks and copies the stack No: only suspend (transformed) frames
    Function colouring None suspend required on the path
    Platform requirement JDK 21+ VM (not ART, not Native) Compiler only: JVM, ART, Native, JS, Wasm
    Suspended-state cost The used stack chunk, copied to the heap Live locals in continuation objects
    Structured cancellation Structured concurrency API was still preview in JDK 21 Built in (Job hierarchy)
    Cold streams No equivalent (you'd need Rx/Reactor) Flow
    Stack traces Natural Need recovery/debug probes
    Virtual threads win on backend ergonomics with blocking libraries. Coroutines win on portability, cancellation and streams, which is exactly what mobile needs.
  6. Fix (recommendation): 
    // Shared (commonMain): unchanged, stackless
interface OrderRepository {
    suspend fun place(order: Order): Receipt
    fun observe(userId: String): Flow<List<Order>>
}

// Backend (jvmMain, JDK 21): blocking JDBC runs on virtual threads, still suspend-callable
val vtDispatcher = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor().asCoroutineDispatcher()
class JdbcOrderRepository(private val ds: DataSource) : OrderRepository {
    override suspend fun place(order: Order) = withContext(vtDispatcher) { insertBlocking(order) }
    override fun observe(userId: String) = flow { /* poll or LISTEN/NOTIFY */ }.flowOn(vtDispatcher)
}
// Android: Room/Retrofit suspend APIs as today; iOS: SKIE/KMP-NativeCoroutines or a wrapper for Swift
  7. Prevention:
    • An ADR documenting the decision and the re-evaluation trigger (for example, if ART ever ships virtual threads).
    • Module boundary lint: no runBlocking in commonMain.
    • Backend monitoring for virtual-thread pinning (JFR jdk.VirtualThreadPinned events).
  8. Trade-offs & what I'd NOT do: Not rewrite 90 suspend functions into blocking ones (it breaks Android and iOS for a backend-only ergonomic gain). Not maintain dual APIs. I accept that backend devs still write suspend and see recovered stack traces. The virtual-thread dispatcher gives them most of the blocking-library benefit.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• "Can't Android just use a big thread pool? We only need tens of tasks." → Capacity, yes. But you lose structured cancellation tied to lifecycles, Flow for Room/DataStore observation, and Main-safety conventions. Those matter far more than raw task counts on mobile.
  • "Isn't withContext(vtDispatcher) double scheduling?" → One extra dispatch per call, microseconds. Negligible next to JDBC round-trips. Measure if the endpoint is ultra-hot.
  • "What about Kotlin/JS and Wasm?" → Single-threaded event loops with no threads to block. Stackless coroutines are the only model that works there, which reinforces option 1.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: A platform team I advised nearly converted a shared KMP module to blocking APIs after a JDK upgrade. The prototype showed the backend gained less than 5% p95 over coroutines on a virtual-thread dispatcher, while the Android port would have lost lifecycle cancellation. The proposal was dropped in one meeting, on the strength of the numbers.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: picks one technology on hype, unaware ART/Native lack virtual threads.
  • Hire: explains stackful vs stackless and recommends keeping coroutines in shared code.
  • Strong hire: gives per-platform recommendations, uses virtual threads as a dispatcher, mentions pinning and the preview status of structured concurrency in JDK 21, quantifies the migration cost (90/40 APIs), and proposes a benchmark plus an ADR with re-evaluation triggers.
